messages.content: My flight into Chicago landed at 14:40 and my connection to Denver left at 15:10 — I reached the gate at 14:55 and the door was already closed. The remaining flights to Denver today are 16:25 (arrives 18:05), 18:40 (arrives 20:20), and 20:15 (arrives 21:55). I have a work event at 20:00 downtown; the airport-to-venue ride is 40 minutes. Replan me.

The 15:10 is gone, so work backwards from the one fixed point: the 20:00 event.

- 18:40 flight lands 20:20 — after the event starts. Eliminated.
- 20:15 flight lands 21:55. Eliminated.
- 16:25 flight lands 18:05. Exit with bags by ~18:25, +40 min ride = 19:05 at the venue. That is 55 minutes early. This is the only option that works.

Revised plan: rebook onto the 16:25 now (boarding ~15:55, so go to the desk first, then coffee). Land 18:05, venue 19:05, event 20:00. Your original plan had you landing at 16:50 with a relaxed evening; the cost of the miss is the buffer, not the event — nothing else in the day has to move.

My 09:30 flight tomorrow was just cancelled. The airline offers a train instead: departs 11:20, journey 3h50, then a 25-minute taxi to my hotel. I have a fixed meeting at 17:00 at an office 15 minutes from the hotel, and dinner at 19:30. Give me the revised plan.

Disruption: flight cancelled. The rail replacement still protects both fixed points — here is the rebuilt day, with every leg checked.

```
11:20  Train departs (arrive station by 10:50)
15:10  Train arrives (11:20 + 3h50)
15:35  Hotel (15:10 + 25 min taxi)
15:35–16:35  Check in, shower, change (60 min)
16:35  Leave hotel
16:50  Office (16:35 + 15 min) — 10 min early
17:00  Meeting (fixed, held)
19:30  Dinner (unchanged)
```

Why it works: the meeting only needs you at the office by 17:00, and the chain delivers you at 16:50 with an hour of hotel time to spare. What changed: you lose the free afternoon the 09:30 flight would have given you (original landing 13:05). What did not change: the meeting and the dinner. No other booking needs to move.

Road trip help. Day 1 is city A. Day 2 was: drive A to B (2h) in the morning, sightsee B, sleep in B. Day 3: drive B to C (45 min) for a fixed 09:00 appointment in C, then drive C back to A (2h45) for a 16:00 flight. The hotel in B just told me night 2 is overbooked — no room. The nearest available room is in C. Replan without dropping the appointment or the flight.

Move the B-to-C drive from Day 3 morning to Day 2 evening — C is where you need to be at 09:00 anyway, so sleeping there is strictly better.

Revised plan:
- Day 2: Drive A to B in the morning as planned (2h), sightsee B until 17:00, then drive B to C (45 min), arriving 17:45. Sleep in C.
- Day 3: You are already in C. The appointment is 15 minutes from the hotel; leave 08:30, arrive 08:45, 15 minutes early for the fixed 09:00.
- After the appointment and lunch, leave C by 12:15. Drive C to A is 2h45, so you reach the airport at 15:00 — a full hour before the 16:00 flight.

Checks: appointment held with buffer, flight held with buffer, and B loses nothing but the overnight. The only real cost is a 17:00 cutoff on Day 2 sightseeing instead of a full evening in B. Book the C room for night 2 now, and tell the B hotel the cancellation is on their overbooking, so no fee should apply.

We're driving over the mountains tomorrow, departing 08:00. Route A via the pass: 180 miles, about 3h30 in clear weather, but snow is forecast from 11:00 and the pass closes at noon. Route B, the low road: 245 miles at an average 55 mph, plus we'll need one 20-minute fuel stop. Sunset is 18:30. Which route, and show me why.

The pass route only works if nothing goes wrong inside a closing weather window. The low road is slower on paper and safer in fact.

```
Route A (pass):  depart 08:00, best case arrive 11:30
  - Snow starts 11:00, pass closes 12:00
  - Any 30-min delay puts you in the storm or at a closed pass
Route B (low):   245 mi / 55 mph = 4h27 driving
  + 20 min fuel stop = 4h47 total
  depart 08:00 -> arrive 12:47
  - Margin to sunset (18:30): 5h43 — irrelevant, you arrive at lunch
```

Decision: Route B, depart 08:00, arrive ~12:47. Route A's best case (11:30) beats B by about an hour, but its failure mode is being turned around at a closed pass and driving B anyway, hours late. B's worst realistic case still lands you in daylight with the whole afternoon intact. The plan only breaks if you chase A's best case.

I missed my 09:10 bus to the station. My train leaves the station at 10:05 and the station is a 25-minute ride away. The next bus is 09:40 and gets in at 10:12. A taxi can pick me up in 10 minutes and costs $28 vs $3 for the bus. What do I do?

Take the taxi — the bus math no longer works. The 09:40 bus arrives at 10:12, which is 7 minutes after your 10:05 train leaves. The taxi: pickup at ~09:20 (10 minutes from now), 25-minute ride, at the station by 09:45. That leaves a 20-minute buffer for the platform and a coffee.

The $25 difference is the whole cost of the miss; everything after the train is unchanged. One adjustment: have the taxi meet you at the corner by the bus stop so there is no confusion about the pickup point, and keep the train ticket's QR code open on your phone while you ride.

My flight now lands at 21:40 instead of 19:10. The rental car desk at the airport closes at 22:30 and reopens at 06:30. Getting off the plane and through baggage takes about 25 minutes. I have a 09:00 meeting tomorrow, 20 minutes from my hotel. Build me a plan with a fallback.

The delay eats your margin but not the plan — as long as you treat 22:30 as a hard wall and pre-position the fallback.

```
PLAN A (flight on its new time)
21:40  Land
22:05  At rental desk (21:40 + 25 min) — 25 min before close
22:20  Drive off; hotel by ~22:50
08:20  Leave hotel -> 08:40 at meeting (09:00, held)

PLAN B (any further slip past ~22:05 at the desk)
Hotel shuttle runs until 23:30 — take it, sleep
06:45  Collect car at reopened desk (06:30)
07:15  Back at hotel, breakfast, change
08:20  Leave -> meeting still held
```

The trigger is explicit: if you are not physically at the desk by 22:05, stop hurrying and switch to Plan B — running for a closing desk helps no one. Do two things now, while airborne: screenshot the rental confirmation for offline access, and note the shuttle pickup point. The meeting never moves in either branch.

A road closure detour just added 45 minutes to our drive. We were due at the ferry dock at 13:40. Ferries leave at 14:00 and 16:30, the crossing is 45 minutes, then it's a 30-minute drive to the restaurant where we have a 19:00 dinner reservation. My partner wants to speed to catch the 14:00. Talk us through it.

Don't speed — the numbers say the 14:00 is already gone, and the 16:30 still makes dinner comfortably.

New dock arrival: 13:40 + 45 min = 14:25. That misses the 14:00 sailing by 25 minutes. Making that up would mean averaging well over the limit for the remaining drive, and you'd still likely watch it leave.

Revised plan on the 16:30 ferry: crossing ends 17:15, 30-minute drive puts you at the restaurant at 17:45 — 75 minutes before your 19:00 reservation. Use the 14:25–16:15 window at the port instead: lunch, fuel, a walk. The detour costs you the port-town afternoon you had planned after arrival, but dinner, the crossing, and the drive all hold. The plan only breaks if you waste the wait being frustrated instead of fed.

Consulting trip, two days. Original: land Day 1 at 12:20, workshop 14:00–16:00 (movable), client dinner 16:30 (fixed). Day 2: board session 09:00 (fixed), site tour 13:00 (movable). My flight is now landing Day 1 at 15:20. Hotel is 35 minutes from the airport, dinner venue is 20 minutes from the hotel, the site is 40 minutes from the airport and my Day 2 flight home is 18:30. Rebuild both days.

Both fixed points survive; the two movable items trade places around them.

```
DAY 1
15:20  Land (was 12:20)
15:55  Hotel (35 min) — bags dropped, no full check-in routine
16:05  Leave hotel
16:25  Dinner venue (20 min) — 5 min early
16:30  Client dinner (FIXED, held)
  -> the 14:00 workshop cannot happen today; it moves to Day 2

DAY 2
09:00  Board session (FIXED, held, unchanged)
13:00–15:00  Workshop (moved here; uses the tour's old slot)
15:15–16:15  Site tour (moved after the workshop)
16:15  Leave site; 40 min to airport -> 16:55
18:30  Flight home (1h35 at the airport — comfortable)
```

Constraint check: the workshop needed a 2-hour block and gets exactly 13:00–15:00; the tour needs to end by 16:15 to protect the flight, and it does. One warning to send the client today: you will arrive at dinner straight from the airport run, so the workshop materials ship by email tonight instead of being hand-carried tomorrow.

There's a train strike Saturday. My train was depart 08:00, arrive 10:10, then a 20-minute taxi to a wedding rehearsal at 11:30. The replacement bus departs 07:35 and arrives 10:40. The bus station is 25 minutes from my home (the train station was 15). The strike is Saturday only; my Sunday return train is fine. Replan Saturday morning.

The rehearsal still holds — your morning just starts earlier and your buffer shrinks.

- Leave home 06:55 (was 07:20): 25 minutes to the bus station gets you there at 07:20, 15 minutes before the 07:35 departure.
- Bus arrives 10:40 (the ride is 3h05 vs the train's 2h10).
- Taxi 20 minutes: at the venue by 11:00.
- Rehearsal 11:30: held, with a 30-minute buffer instead of the original 60.

Nothing else moves: the rehearsal, the wedding, and the Sunday return are untouched. Two practical notes: book the bus seat today, because every other train passenger has the same idea; and put the taxi company's number in your phone now, since 10:40 on a strike Saturday is peak chaos at that station.

Disaster: our rented 7-seat van broke down at 09:00. Six of us need to get 200 miles to an event that starts at 15:00. We have a sedan (5 seats, trunk fits 4 large cases) and a hatchback (4 seats, fits 2 large cases). We have 6 large cases. Only Ana and Tom are insured to drive. Average speed for the trip is about 50 mph and we want one 15-minute stop. Build the replacement plan.

Two cars replace one van. Capacity, luggage, drivers, and time all check out — with 65 minutes to spare.

```
PEOPLE (6 travellers, 2 drivers)
Car A (sedan, Ana drives): Ana + 3 passengers = 4 of 5 seats
Car B (hatchback, Tom drives): Tom + 2 passengers = 3 of 4 seats
Total seats used 7 of 9 — everyone fits, nobody is split from a seatbelt

LUGGAGE (6 large cases)
Sedan trunk: 4 cases | Hatchback: 2 cases | Total 6 of 6 — exact fit

TIMELINE
09:00–09:40  Transfer people and cases to the two cars
09:40  Depart
09:40–13:40  200 mi at 50 mph = 4h00 driving
+ 15 min stop -> arrive 13:55
15:00  Event (FIXED) — 65 min buffer
```

Driver check: 4 hours each is well within a safe single stint, and each car has a licensed, insured driver — that constraint, not seats, was the binding one. Load the sedan with the four heaviest cases (lower, more stable) and keep one shared case with everyone's event clothes in Car A, so even a separation en route can't strand anyone without their outfit. The van company gets a breakdown claim; that paperwork waits until after the event.

The airline rebooked me onto a red-eye landing at 06:10 tomorrow. I have a fixed presentation at 10:00 at my office. Home is 45 minutes from the airport, the office is 25 minutes from the airport and opens at 07:00. I'll probably sleep about 3 hours on the plane (roughly 23:00–02:00). Airport hotel is a 5-minute shuttle. What's the smartest morning?

Skip the hotel nap — it buys 1h45 of sleep and sells your safety margin. Go straight to the office.

The options, timed:
- Airport hotel: exit by 06:40, shuttle, asleep ~07:00–08:45, leave 09:30, office 09:55. Five minutes before a fixed presentation, after a red-eye. One slow shuttle and you're late and groggy.
- Home: arrive 07:25, leave again 09:15 to reach the office 09:40. No real sleep available in that window anyway.
- Office early (chosen): land 06:10, exit 06:40, at the office 07:05. Rest in the quiet room until 08:30, shower in the gym locker room, coffee, then use 08:45–09:45 for a calm final run-through.

Your 3 hours of plane sleep plus 90 minutes of office rest is survivable for one morning, and you present at 10:00 having been in the building for three hours — zero commute risk. Put the presentation first in your day and push everything else to the afternoon; crash after lunch, not before the talk.

We're based in a small town for two day trips. Monday was the coastal town (the museum is the whole point), Tuesday the vineyard. I just learned the museum is closed Mondays, and the vineyard is closed Tuesdays. Both drives are 1h15 each way. Fix the week.

Swap the days — each trip lands on the day its attraction is actually open.

- Monday: vineyard. It is closed Tuesdays but open Mondays, so it takes Monday's slot.
- Tuesday: coastal town and museum. The museum is closed Mondays but open Tuesday through Sunday, so Tuesday works.

Both drives are the same 1h15 each way, so no timing changes at all: leave at 09:00 both days as planned, home by early evening both days. The only admin is swapping the two lunch reservations — the vineyard restaurant booking moves from Tuesday to Monday and the coastal cafe from Monday to Tuesday. Call both today; a swap is much easier to get than a new booking. Original plan had you driving to a locked museum on Monday; the fixed week loses nothing.

Border crossing took 2 hours longer than planned — we got through at 16:10 instead of 14:10. We still have 180 km to drive (realistic average 90 km/h). Our cruise check-in closes at 19:00 and boarding ends at 19:15; parking is 15 minutes from the terminal. We'd planned a 45-minute scenic stop and a fuel stop; the tank shows 260 km of range. Can we still make the ship?

Yes — but only by cutting both planned stops. Here is the arithmetic:

- Drive: 180 km at 90 km/h = 2h00. Depart the border 16:10, reach the port town at 18:10.
- Parking by 18:25, terminal by 18:40 (15-minute walk/transfer).
- Check-in closes 19:00: you are in with 20 minutes to spare. Boarding ends 19:15: held.

What has to go: the 45-minute scenic stop (keeping it puts you at the terminal at 19:25, after boarding ends — that alone sinks the plan) and the fuel stop, which you don't need: 260 km of range against 180 km of driving leaves an 80 km reserve. Eat on board instead of at the scenic stop.

One discipline rule for the drive: the 20-minute margin assumes no further delays, so if anything else eats more than 15 minutes — a queue, a wrong turn — call the cruise line from the road; ships will sometimes hold check-in for a caller they know is close, but only if they hear from you before 19:00.

Ski trip replan. We have a 2-day lift pass for Wednesday and Thursday. A storm is now forecast to close the upper lifts all Wednesday; Thursday is clear. Our ski lesson (fixed, on the lower mountain, runs in any weather) is Wednesday 10:00–12:00. Rentals were to be picked up Wednesday 09:00 and returned Friday 09:00, and we have a dinner reservation Wednesday 19:00. Rebuild the two days.

The storm only kills Wednesday's upper lifts, so Wednesday becomes the skills-and-village day and Thursday carries the full mountain.

```
WEDNESDAY (storm, upper lifts closed)
09:00  Rental pickup (unchanged) — go early, everyone has the same idea
10:00–12:00  Lesson, lower mountain (FIXED, runs in any weather)
12:00–16:00  Lower-lift practice runs + village afternoon
19:00  Dinner reservation (unchanged)

THURSDAY (clear)
09:00–16:00  Full-mountain ski day — use the pass day that matters
             most here; upper lifts open
FRIDAY
09:00  Rental return (unchanged)
```

Pass check: ask the ticket desk today to confirm the 2-day pass works as two any-days rather than consecutive days; if it is consecutive-only, Wednesday still counts as used on the lower lifts, which the lesson day does anyway. Nothing booked is lost: lesson, dinner, and rental return all stay exactly where they were.

Our excursion bus broke down at 14:50, about a 40-minute drive from the port. The ship's all-aboard is 16:30 and it sails at 17:00. There are 24 of us. Taxis seat 4, cost $45 each, and can reach us in about 25 minutes. The tour operator's policy covers transport failures. It's 18 miles — walking is not real, right? Replan the get-back.

Right, walking is not real: 18 miles is a 6-hour walk against a 100-minute window. Taxis are the plan, and the numbers work if you order now.

- Capacity: 24 passengers / 4 per taxi = 6 taxis. Order all 6 immediately.
- Timeline: taxis arrive ~15:15 (25 min), load fast, 40-minute drive, at the port ~15:55.
- All-aboard is 16:30: you arrive with 35 minutes to spare.

Cost: 6 × $45 = $270, and per the operator's stated policy on transport failures, that is their bill, not yours — keep every receipt and the breakdown photo with the time visible. Two execution details: the tour guide rides in the last taxi and counts heads at the port against the group list of 24, because the one real risk in this plan is leaving someone at a broken bus, not the drive. And send one person ahead in the first taxi to tell the gangway the group is coming, so the ship knows the 24 are inbound well before 16:30.

My return flight got moved a day later. Option 1: change my existing ticket — $75 change fee plus $60 fare difference, and my hotel booking stays at 3 nights × $140. Option 2: buy a new ticket for $310 on the original day, get a $190 credit (not cash) for the cancelled one, and drop to 2 hotel nights. Meals per diem is capped at $60/day either way. Which is cheaper, honestly?

Option 1 wins on cash, and it isn't close. The trick is not letting the $190 credit masquerade as money.

```
OPTION 1 — change the ticket
Change fee $75 + fare difference $60      = $135 cash
Hotel: 3 nights x $140                    = $420
Total new cash                            = $555

OPTION 2 — new ticket, one less night
New ticket                                = $310 cash
Hotel: 2 nights x $140                    = $280 cash
Total new cash                            = $590
Minus $190 credit (future travel only, not cash)
```

Comparison: Option 1 costs $555 cash; Option 2 costs $590 cash and leaves you holding a $190 credit you may or may not use before it expires. Option 2 only wins if you are certain to spend that credit on travel you'd take anyway — and even then it wins on value, not cash, by $155 at the price of a day of your trip. Meals are a wash: the per diem cap is $60/day under both, and Option 1's extra day is capped the same way. Take Option 1, and spend the saved afternoon on the extra day instead of at an airport.

My friend's flight just got delayed 90 minutes — landing 19:30 instead of 18:00. My evening was: gym 17:30–18:15, groceries (store closes 21:00), drive 35 minutes to the airport, then a restaurant dinner. The restaurant's kitchen closes at 21:30 and it seats last parties at 20:45. Replan the evening.

Everything survives except the restaurant — replace it with cooking at home, which your grocery run already covers.

- Gym 17:30–18:15: unchanged.
- Groceries 18:30–19:00: unchanged slot, but shop for dinner ingredients now, not just the weekly list.
- Leave for the airport 19:05, arrive 19:40. Your friend lands 19:30 and needs ~20 minutes to exit, so you meet at ~19:50 with almost no waiting.
- Home by ~20:30. The restaurant is dead on this timeline: you'd reach it at ~20:35 at the absolute earliest from the airport, against a 20:45 last seating, with zero margin — don't build an evening on that.

Dinner at home at ~21:00 from the groceries you already bought. Net cost of the delay: one restaurant reservation (call and cancel it from the airport so you don't no-show), and nothing else.

EV road trip. The charger we planned to use at mile 120 is offline. We're at mile 60 showing 95 miles of range. The next working charger is at mile 150. Slowing from 70 mph to 55 mph stretches the range to about 115 miles. After that charger, the next leg is 130 miles; a charge there takes 30 minutes, and we were going to have lunch during the mile-120 stop. Hotel check-in is any time before 18:00 and we'd originally estimated a 14:20 arrival. Rebuild the leg.

Slowing down converts an impossible leg into a comfortable one, at a cost of 21 minutes.

```
THE PROBLEM LEG (mile 60 -> mile 150 = 90 miles)
At 70 mph: range 95 mi vs 90 mi needed = 5 mi margin — too thin
At 55 mph: range ~115 mi vs 90 mi needed = ~25 mi margin — safe
Time at 55 mph: 90 / 55 = 1h38 (vs 1h17 at 70) -> +21 min

REVISED PLAN
Now–mile 150: drive at 55, arrive with ~25 mi in hand
Mile 150: charge 30 min — lunch moves here (was mile 120)
Next leg: 130 mi; charge to at least 140 mi of range before leaving
Arrival: 14:20 + 21 min = ~14:45
Hotel check-in deadline 18:00 — held with 3h+ to spare
```

Stop count is unchanged (one charging stop, just relocated), and lunch still happens during a charge, exactly as designed. The only real change is cruising speed for 90 miles and a ~14:45 arrival. Check the charger after mile 150 is reporting online before you leave this one — the whole plan rests on single chargers now, so verify each next hop before departing the current one.

Our keynote speaker just cancelled at 09:00 for today's event, 13:00–17:00. Original agenda: keynote 60 min, panel 45, break 15, workshops 60, closing 30, networking 30. Two of the panelists have agreed to do a fireside conversation instead if we give them a slot. Rebuild the agenda to fill the same 13:00–17:00 block.

The 240-minute block can be refilled exactly — extend what you have and let the fireside take the keynote's slot at reduced length.

```
REVISED AGENDA (13:00–17:00 = 240 min)
13:00–13:30  Fireside conversation (two panelists)   30
13:30–14:30  Panel (extended from 45)                60
14:30–14:45  Break                                   15
14:45–16:00  Workshops (extended from 60)            75
16:00–16:30  Closing                                 30
16:30–17:00  Networking                              30
Total                                               240
```

Check against the original: 60+45+15+60+30+30 = 240; the revision sums to the same 240, so doors, catering, and room booking are untouched. The keynote's 60 minutes are absorbed by the fireside (30) plus 15 extra each for the panel and workshops. Announce it as a format change, not an apology tour: one line in the opening remarks, the printed agenda gets a sticker, and the app schedule updates before doors. The workshops gaining 15 minutes is a genuine upgrade — tell the facilitators by 10:00 so they can stretch their exercises rather than pad.

Venue disaster: our booked hall is unusable and the replacement room has a legal capacity of 200 standing but only 160 seated for dinner. We have 180 confirmed guests. The room has 120 chairs available, a 40-foot wall for serving stations, and space for a 16x16 ft dance floor. The plan was a seated dinner. Fix the format.

A seated dinner for 180 is physically impossible in this room — 160 seats is the legal seated limit, and you have 180 confirmed guests. Change the format, not the guest list.

Revised format: reception style.
- Capacity check: 180 guests ≤ 200 standing limit. Legal.
- Seating: the 120 available chairs go out as lounge clusters and perimeter seating, with 40 of them reserved and signed for elderly guests and anyone who needs to sit — everyone else circulates, which is normal for a reception.
- Food: serving stations instead of plated courses. Four 8-foot station tables = 32 feet along the 40-foot wall — fits with room for the drinks station at the end.
- Dance floor: 16x16 ft as planned; it no longer competes with dining tables, so it actually gets bigger in practice.

What you must do today: tell the caterer the words 'stations, not plated' (their staffing and timing change completely), and send guests a one-line note — 'cocktail-style reception, seating throughout' — so nobody arrives expecting a table place card. The event keeps its date, its guests, and its menu items; only the furniture logic changes.

Wedding Saturday: 140 guests, ceremony was outdoors at 16:00 on the lawn, reception in a tent. Rain now forecast from 15:00 all evening. The barn hall seats 150 and its foyer can hold a cocktail hour; flipping the hall from ceremony to dinner setup takes 6 staff about 45 minutes. Sunset photos were planned for 19:40. Rebuild the day.

Rain moves everything indoors, and the flip window hides inside the cocktail hour. The hall's 150 seats cover your 140 guests with 10 to spare.

```
REVISED TIMELINE
14:30–15:10  Photos in the garden — moved BEFORE the rain (was 19:40 sunset set)
16:00–16:30  Ceremony in the barn hall
16:30–17:15  Cocktail hour in the foyer
             (6 staff flip the hall in these exact 45 min)
17:30–19:00  Dinner in the flipped hall (140 seated of 150 capacity)
19:00–22:00  Dancing — hall again, no further flip needed
21:55        Sparkler exit under the barn's covered porch
```

What changed: the ceremony's location, the photos' time, and nothing else — the 16:00 start, the dinner menu, and the guest count are untouched. Two things to arrange today: tell the photographer the garden session moved to 14:30 (the couple needs to be ready 90 minutes earlier, which is the one real cost of this plan), and confirm the foyer bar setup so 140 people with drinks aren't blocking the flip crew's doors. The sunset photos are the only genuine loss; the 14:30 garden set replaces them, not replicates them.
Kids' birthday party today, 14:00–16:00. The magician (booked 14:30–15:15) just cancelled at 12:30. Food was pizza arriving 15:00 and cake at 15:15, piñata at 15:30, pickup at 16:00. Save the party.

The party survives on re-sequencing — you have 90 minutes to prep, and everything the magician was covering can be covered by moving food earlier and running one parent-led activity.

Revised running order:
- 14:00 Arrivals and free play (unchanged)
- 14:20–14:45 Scavenger hunt in the garden — this replaces the magician's slot energy; write 10 items on a card during your 90 minutes of prep
- 14:45 Pizza and cake — call the pizza place now and move delivery from 15:00 to 14:40
- 15:15 Party games (musical statues, pass-the-parcel — prep the parcel in your 90 minutes too)
- 15:45 Piñata (moved from 15:30)
- 16:00 Pickup (unchanged)

Total still exactly two hours, no gap longer than a room of seven-year-olds can survive. The two phone calls that matter: pizza place (delivery time) and the magician (refund of the deposit, since they cancelled). Everything else is cards, a wrapped parcel, and confidence.

Training day tomorrow, 09:00–16:00, was designed for two facilitators running parallel tracks A and B. One facilitator is sick. The four core sessions are 75 minutes each; the day has a 45-minute lunch and two 15-minute breaks. A duplicated case-study session ran in both tracks. Rebuild the day for one facilitator without losing any core topic.

Merging the tracks keeps all four core topics — the duplicated case study is the casualty, and it was redundant by design.

```
MERGED DAY (09:00–16:00 = 420 min)
09:00–10:15  Session 1 (core)        75
10:15–10:30  Break                   15
10:30–11:45  Session 2 (core)        75
11:45–12:30  Lunch                   45
12:30–13:45  Session 3 (core)        75
13:45–14:00  Break                   15
14:00–15:15  Session 4 (core)        75
15:15–16:00  Combined exercise + close  45
Instruction: 75x4 + 45 = 345 | Breaks: 15+45+15 = 75 | Total 420 ✓
```

What changed: attendees get all four core sessions in sequence instead of choosing tracks, and the case study runs once, inside the combined exercise, instead of twice in parallel. What it costs: the track choice and the smaller-group feel — mitigate by running the combined exercise in table groups of six with the facilitator rotating. Email attendees tonight: one room, one agenda, same start and end times, so nobody walks into the wrong track room at 09:00.

Catering emergency: 90 guests, dinner service at 19:00, and at 17:45 the caterer tells me the mains only cover 50 people — we're 40 servings short. The sides, however, are full portions for 90. A local deli can sell me trays of 12 servings at $95 each, ready for pickup in 45 minutes; the round trip is 25 minutes. A restaurant quoted $640 for an emergency order. Fix dinner.

Buy the deli trays — the arithmetic and the clock both favor them.

- Shortfall: 90 − 50 = 40 servings.
- Trays: 4 trays × 12 servings = 48 servings — covers the 40 with 8 to spare for seconds and the inevitable dropped plate. Cost: 4 × $95 = $380, against the restaurant's $640. You save $260.
- Clock: order at ~17:50, ready in 45 minutes (18:35), 25-minute round trip means a volunteer leaves at 18:20 and is back by ~18:45 — 15 minutes before the 19:00 service. The caterer's 50 mains and the full sides hold fine until then.

Execution: send the volunteer at 18:20 with a car already warmed and the deli's address in their phone; meanwhile the caterer plates their 50 mains as the first wave and the deli trays become the second wave, presented as a buffet top-up rather than an admission. Guests will read it as abundance. Separately, and after tonight: the caterer's contract said 90 — the $380 deli bill goes to them with the receipt.

School play tonight: doors 18:30, show 19:00. At 15:00 the lead actor went home ill. The understudy knows all the lines but has never done the Act 2 dance in position. The choreographer can simplify the dance. The costume needs 20 minutes of alteration for the understudy. Build the afternoon.

Conference AV failure: the main hall (300 seats) projector is dead. The AV tech estimates the projector is fixed by 13:30. The day must end by 15:30 with a 30-minute closing. Save the day.

You can't move 280 people into a 120-seat room, so move time instead of people — and notice the panel needs no projector at all.

Revised day:
- 10:00, main hall: the panel moves here and runs first. 90 people in 300 seats, zero slides needed — the dead projector is irrelevant to it.
- 10:00, breakout room: the workshop runs as planned (40 people, unchanged).
- 12:30 Lunch (unchanged).
- 13:30–13:50 AV tech finishes and you test the projector with the actual keynote deck.
- 14:00–15:00 Keynote in the main hall, slides working, all 280 seated.
- 15:00–15:30 Closing, ending on time.

The swap that makes it work: the keynote speaker does a short on-stage interview during the panel slot's Q&A if they're willing, so the audience still sees them in the morning. What you must not do is start the slide-heavy keynote at 10:00 on a dead projector and hope.

Festival tonight: gates 17:00, venue curfew is a hard 23:00. Original sets: opener 18:00–18:45, Band 2 19:15–20:15, headliner 20:45–22:30, with 30-minute changeovers. The headliner can play 105 minutes but not their full set. Rebuild the running order.

Swap the top two acts and give the closing slot to the band that can stretch. Curfew is the hard wall; everything is built backwards from 23:00.

```
REVISED RUNNING ORDER
17:00        Gates (unchanged)
18:00–18:45  Opener                     45 min
18:45–19:15  Changeover                 30 min
19:15–21:00  Headliner (moved earlier) 105 min — full set minus encore

Tell the audience at gates via the app and stage screens — 'headliner at 19:15 tonight' — because the one failure mode left is 2,000 people drifting to food trucks at 20:30 expecting the headliner at 20:45.

Dinner party in 3 hours. I planned a pasta bake for 8 (800g pasta, sauce to match) and my table seats 8. A guest just told me they're bringing three extra people — 11 total, including 2 kids. I have 1kg of pasta in the cupboard. Fix dinner.

Scale the bake by 1.5 and split the seating — the cupboard is one bag short, so the shopping list is short too.

Food: 11 people vs the recipe's 8 is a factor of about 1.4; round to 1.5× for safety. Pasta needed: 800g × 1.5 = 1,200g. You have 1,000g, so buy one 500g bag (you'll use 200g of it) and scale the sauce ingredients by 1.5 as well. One bigger dish or two dishes — if your dish only fits the 8-person bake, make two: the main bake plus a smaller one, staggered 10 minutes apart in the same oven.

Seating: the table seats 8. The 2 kids eat at the kitchen counter (they will prefer this, honestly), leaving 9 adults — table of 8 plus one folding chair at the corner. Total: 8 + 1 + 2 = 11. ✓

Timing check: a 20-minute store run still leaves you 2h40, and a pasta bake needs about an hour including assembly. Text the guest back warmly and ask the one useful question: any allergies among the three? Better to know before the bake is built.

Charity gala tonight. Original program: reception 18:30, dinner 19:15–20:15, live auction 20:15, dessert and awards 21:15, close 22:00, and the venue requires us out by 22:30. The auctioneer is delayed and can't start before 21:00. The live auction has 16 lots that take about 5 minutes each. The silent auction was due to close at 20:00. Rebuild the evening.

Move awards before the auction, stretch the silent auction into the gap, and trim the live auction to the lots that earn their minutes.

```
REVISED PROGRAM
18:30  Reception (unchanged)
19:15–20:15  Dinner (unchanged)
20:15–21:00  Awards + appeal video (moved UP from 21:15)
21:00–22:00  Live auction: 12 lots x 5 min = 60 min
             (4 lowest-value lots move to the silent auction)

```

Why each move works: the silent auction extension covers the 20:15–21:00 gap with something guests can actually do, and moving 4 lots into it raises its total. The live auction at 12 lots × 5 minutes is exactly 60 minutes — 16 lots would have needed 80 and broken the 22:30 wall, so the cut is arithmetic, not taste. The auctioneer gets a 21:00 start that respects their delay, and dessert served at tables during the auction means no separate dessert slot is needed. Announce the reorder during dinner service, once, by the MC.

School sports day: the field is flooded. We have 4 groups of kids and 9:00–12:00. The plan was 6 outdoor stations. We have a hall and a gym indoors. Rotations need 5 minutes of moving time between stations. Rebuild the morning with stations that work indoors.

Time budget: 9:00–12:00 = 180 minutes. Opening and closing take 30, leaving 150 = 6 rotations × 25 minutes (20 minutes of activity + 5 minutes to move). ✓ Four groups rotate through six stations, so two stations rest each round — use those for the equipment-heavy resets.

Indoor station swaps:
- Sprint → 20-metre shuttle runs in the hall (measure and cone it)
- Long jump → standing long jump onto gym mats
- Throwing → foam javelin / beanbag target throw in the gym
- Hurdles → agility ladder and cone slalom
- Distance run → continuous relay laps of the hall
- Obstacle course → benches, mats, and tunnels in the gym (mostly unchanged — it was always the indoor-friendly one)

Points scoring carries over exactly, so the day still produces the same winners and the same trophy moment at 11:45. Tell the kids at the 9:00 assembly it's 'indoor championships rules' — same competition, different floor.

Two-day retreat, days run 09:00–17:00 with a 1-hour lunch and two 30-minute breaks. Speaker S was Day 2: her talk T (90 min) in the morning and her workshop W (2 hours) in the afternoon — W explicitly builds on T. Speaker R has a standalone 90-minute talk booked for Day 3. S just told us she cannot come Day 2 but can come Day 3; R can move to Day 2. Day 2 also had an independent case clinic (90 min), Day 3 an independent open lab (60 min) and closing (60 min). Rebuild both days keeping T before W.

Swap the speakers' days wholesale — moving S's talk without her workshop would break the one hard dependency in the programme: W builds on T.

```
DAY 2 (R's day now)                    DAY 3 (S's day now)
09:00–10:30  R talk (standalone)       09:00–10:30  Talk T (S)
10:30–11:00  Break                     10:30–11:00  Break
11:00–12:30  Panel (unchanged)         11:00–12:30  Deep-dive Q&A on T
12:30–13:30  Lunch                     12:30–13:30  Lunch
13:30–15:00  Case clinic (independent) 13:30–15:30  Workshop W (builds on T ✓)

16:30–17:00  Day 2 wrap
Both days: sessions + breaks + lunch fill 09:00–17:00 exactly
```

Dependency check: T (Day 3, 09:00) still precedes W (Day 3, 13:30) — on the same day, which is actually tighter teaching than the original split. The case clinic and open lab are independent, so they fill Day 2's afternoon without referencing either speaker. What attendees lose: nothing in content; what changes is only which day they hear which speaker. Send the revised programme today with one honest line — 'S and R have swapped days' — so nobody plans travel around the old order.

Wedding at 15:00 today. At 09:00 the florist delivered white roses; we ordered blush. We need: 1 bride bouquet, 4 bridesmaid bouquets, 8 centerpieces. The florist can get blush roses from a wholesaler by 12:30 for a $60 rush fee (a full reorder would be $400). We have the white roses and greenery in hand. Photos are at 13:45. Make the morning work.

Split the work: build what white roses can carry now, and reserve the blush for the bouquets people hold in photographs.

- 09:00–10:30 Build the 8 centerpieces with the white roses and greenery. The bride already approved white-with-greenery as her fallback look for table arrangements, and centerpieces are background in photos.
- 10:30 Decision point — but make the call now instead: pay the $60 rush fee. It is $340 less than the $400 full reorder and it saves the one thing that can't be faked, the bride's bouquet.
- 12:30 Blush roses arrive. 12:30–13:30 the florist and an assistant build 5 bouquets: at ~12 minutes each that's 60 minutes of work with two pairs of hands running in parallel — done by ~13:15.
- 13:45 Photos, 15:00 ceremony: both hold with margin.

What not to do: wait until 12:30 to start everything (the centerpieces would collide with the bouquets and the photos), or send the white roses back — they're already your centerpiece solution. The $60 fee and a calm morning beat a perfect-color panic.

Community meeting tonight, room booked 18:00–20:00 and we must be out at 20:00. Our interpreter just cancelled. About 40% of attendees are Spanish-speaking. Our co-chair is bilingual but translating everything consecutively would add about 50% to every item. The agenda has 5 items planned at 15 minutes each, plus we wanted 20 minutes of open Q&A. Two of the items are low-priority updates. Rebuild the agenda.

Consecutive translation of everything doesn't fit — 5 items at 15 min × 1.5 = ~113 minutes before Q&A, against 120 total. So translate the decisions, carry the updates on paper, and defer the rest.

```
REVISED AGENDA (18:00–20:00 = 120 min)
Before 17:30  Volunteer translates the 2 low-priority updates
              into a one-page bilingual handout
18:00–18:10  Welcome + handout explained (updates taken as read)
18:10–19:25  3 decision items x 25 min each = 75 min
             (15 min discussion + 10 min Spanish summary & questions
              per item — summaries, not full consecutive translation)
19:25–19:50  Open Q&A (25 min, co-chair summarizes questions both ways)
19:50–20:00  Close + out on time
Total: 10 + 75 + 25 + 10 = 120 ✓
```

The honest cost: the two deferred updates get a handout instead of a discussion — acceptable for updates, unacceptable for decisions, which is why the three decision items keep full bilingual treatment. Ask the co-chair to summarize rather than translate verbatim; that is what brings each item in at 25 minutes instead of 30+.

Our product launch livestream is at 14:00 today on Platform A, which just went down (it's 12:00). We have a backup YouTube channel. 1,200 people registered; the registration list is exportable from Platform A even during the outage. We have 2 moderators and a 30-minute rehearsal was planned for 13:00. Move the launch.

The launch survives at 14:00 — the platform changes, the hour doesn't. Here is the two-hour drill:

- 12:15 Decision made (now): backup channel it is. No waiting to see if Platform A recovers — a maybe-recovery at 13:45 would leave no rehearsal at all.
- 12:30 Email all 1,200 registrants the new link, and export the registration list first so the email can actually go.
- 12:45 Social posts + pinned link on the community page. Realistically ~40% of registrants will see the email by 14:00, so the link must live in several places.
- 13:00 New link live for sound and camera check.
- By 13:15 Both moderators have accounts and mod rights on the backup channel — this is the step everyone forgets.
- 13:30–14:00 Rehearsal on the new platform (moved from 13:00; the check at 13:00 absorbs the difference).
- 14:00 Go live, on time.

The backup channel records the stream, so the replay asset survives too. After today: the real fix is collecting registrations on infrastructure you control, so a platform outage can never hold your audience list hostage again.

Project plan: Task A (design) runs days 1–3. Task B (build) runs days 4–5 and depends on A plus a supplier input. Task C (testing) runs days 6–9 and depends on B. Launch is day 10. A documentation task (3 days, independent of everything) was scheduled for days 6–8. The supplier input for B just slipped by 2 days — it now arrives on day 6 instead of day 4. Recompute the schedule, name the new critical path, and tell me if anything can claw time back.

The slip passes straight through B and C to the launch, because that chain has zero float. One recovery exists: test preparation can overlap B.

```
ORIGINAL          REVISED (no recovery)     REVISED (with recovery)
A:      days 1–3  A:      days 1–3          A:      days 1–3
(input) day 4     (input) day 6             (input) day 6
B:      days 4–5  B:      days 6–7          B:      days 6–7
C:      days 6–9  C:      days 8–11         C:      days 8–10*
Launch: day 10    Launch: day 12            Launch: day 11
Docs:   days 6–8  Docs:   days 6–8          Docs:   days 6–8
* test-case writing (normally C's first day) happens days 6–7,
  in parallel with B, so C's execution phase starts ready
```

New critical path: A → supplier wait → B → C → launch. The documentation task is not on it — it has float and stays at days 6–8 untouched, which is why throwing the docs writer at the problem wouldn't help. Net position: launch moves from day 10 to day 11 with the recovery, day 12 without. The decision to take today: approve the test team starting test-case work during B (they'll need B's interface spec on day 6, not day 8), and tell stakeholders launch is day 11 — quoting day 12 'to be safe' just hides the one day of recovery you actually found.

It's deadline week — client walkthrough is Friday 14:00 and everything must be finished by then. Priya is out sick all week. Her tasks: data cleanup 5h, charts 4h, appendix 3h. The rest of us have spare capacity beyond our own work: Marco 6h, Jen 8h, Tom 4h. Redistribute Priya's work so nobody is overloaded and Friday holds.

Priya's 12 hours fit inside the team's 18 spare hours — with room, if you split by skill rather than evenly.

- Marco (6h spare): data cleanup, 3h of the 5h. Running total 3h, spare left 3h.
- Tom (4h spare): the remaining 2h of cleanup. Running total 2h, spare left 2h.
- Jen (8h spare): charts 4h + appendix 3h = 7h. Spare left 1h.

Check: 3 + 2 + 7 = 12h — all of Priya's work covered; nobody exceeds capacity (Marco 3/6, Tom 2/4, Jen 7/8).

Why this split: Jen builds the charts because she'll present them at Friday's 14:00 walkthrough — the person presenting should be the person who made them. Cleanup splits across Marco and Tom because it's the only task that divides cleanly without handoff cost. Jen's single spare hour is your contingency: protect it, because if anything in deadline week slips, it will slip into Jen's hour, not into a new crisis. Priya gets one message — 'covered, get well' — and no questions until she's back.

We need 500 units by Monday to fill orders. Our supplier can only ship 320 on Friday. A substitute product is available: 180+ units at $14 each vs $11 for the standard, minimum order 150. If orders ship late instead, we pay a $9 late penalty per order on up to 180 orders. Restocking from the main supplier for the balance would arrive Wednesday. Decide with numbers.

Buy exactly 180 substitute units. It is the cheapest option by a factor of three, and it keeps Monday's promise intact.

```
THE GAP: 500 needed − 320 shipped = 180 units short

OPTION 1 — substitute for the gap (CHOSEN)
Buy 180 x $14 = $2,520 (vs $1,980 at standard price)
Extra cost over standard: 180 x ($14 − $11) = $540
Meets the 150 minimum order ✓ | All 500 ship Monday ✓

OPTION 2 — split-ship and wait for Wednesday restock
180 orders ship late: 180 x $9 penalty = $1,620
Plus refund/discount pressure the penalty doesn't capture

OPTION 3 — ship 320, cancel 180 orders
$0 penalty, but 180 lost sales and the customers with them
```

Decision math: $540 of extra unit cost versus $1,620 of penalties — Option 1 wins by $1,080 before counting goodwill. Order the 180 today so they arrive with Friday's 320, and log the substitute under its own SKU: if a customer asks why their unit differs slightly, you want the answer to be a lookup, not an investigation.

Saturday's server migration window just got cut from 6 hours to 3 hours (22:00–01:00). The steps: snapshot 20 min, database migration 70 min, app deploy 25 min, smoke tests 30 min. We also had planned an analytics backfill (90 min) and a search reindex (45 min) inside the window. Rollback takes 25 minutes. Rebuild the window.

The core migration fits in 180 minutes with the rollback reserve protected — the backfill and reindex don't belong in a window at all, and this cut is the excuse to evict them.

Revised window (22:00–01:00 = 180 min):
- 22:00–22:20 Snapshot (20)
- 22:20–23:30 Database migration (70)
- 23:30–23:55 App deploy (25)
- 23:55–00:25 Smoke tests (30)
- 00:25–01:00 Reserve: 35 minutes held for rollback
Total committed: 145 min + 35 reserve = 180 ✓

Rollback rule, decided now rather than at midnight: if smoke tests have not begun by 00:20, roll back. Rollback takes 25 minutes, so starting it at 00:20 finishes by 00:45, inside the window. If smoke tests are running by 00:20, you have until 00:35 to call it and still land by 01:00.

The evicted work: the analytics backfill (90 min) runs as an online job on Sunday — it never needed downtime. The search reindex (45 min) runs incrementally after the window against the live index. Both were using the window as a convenience, and convenience is what a 3-hour window can't afford.

Rain has pushed the pour to Thursday May 7. Everyone's panicking about the finish date. Work out what actually happens.

Pour          Tue May 5       Thu May 7       rain (+2 days)
Curing (3d)   May 6, 7, 8     May 8, 9, 10    Fri, Sat, Sun —
                                              curing counts calendar
                                              days, not work days
Framing       May 11–14       May 11–14       unchanged: cure is done
                                              Sunday night, crew starts
                                              Monday as booked
Inspection    Fri May 15      Fri May 15      unchanged (Tue/Fri only)
Drywall       May 18–20       May 18–20       unchanged
Finish        Fri May 22      Fri May 22      UNCHANGED
```

The pour slipped into the only two days the schedule could absorb for free: the cure period was always going to span a weekend, it just spans it from the other side now. Two things to do with this gift: confirm the framing crew keeps its May 11 booking (they may assume the whole job slid — tell them today it didn't), and use the found slack to pre-position drywall materials on site during framing week, so May 18 starts with zero delivery risk. The finish date survives; protect it by communicating that it does.

Retail Saturday: we need 28 staff-hours of floor coverage (9:00–13:00 two staff, 13:00–17:00 three staff, 17:00–21:00 two staff). We had 32 hours scheduled. Two people called out: Ana (8h) and Ben (6h). Options: part-timer Kim can add up to 6h, the manager can cover the floor up to 3h, and Lee can extend by 1h. Can we cover the day?

Just barely — every available lever has to be pulled, and they sum exactly to the requirement.

The hole: 32 scheduled − 8 (Ana) − 6 (Ben) = 18 hours remaining against 28 needed. Shortfall: 10 hours.

The fill:
- Kim adds 6h → 24
- Manager covers floor 3h → 27
- Lee extends 1h → 28 ✓

Total: 18 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 28 hours — coverage met exactly, with zero slack. Place them where the day is heaviest: Kim takes the full 13:00–17:00 peak block plus 2 hours of the morning, the manager's 3 floor hours go to the peak too, and Lee's extra hour extends the evening so the close isn't single-staffed.

Zero slack means one more call-out breaks the day, so decide the fallback now: if anyone else drops, the store closes at 20:00 instead of 21:00, which trims the requirement by 2 hours (17:00–20:00 at two staff = 6h instead of 8h). Post that decision in the group chat today, not at 08:55 on Saturday.

A client just pulled our report deadline from Friday 17:00 to Thursday 17:00. The work: analysis 6h, drafting 5h, internal review 3h, revisions 2h, design polish 2h — 18 hours total. Available focused time: Wednesday 6h, Thursday 8h (9:00–17:00), and the analyst can give 2 hours Tuesday evening. The reviewer can comment live in the document, which shrinks revisions. Rebuild the schedule so Thursday 17:00 holds.

18 hours of work, 16 hours of capacity — the plan closes the gap by cutting 2 hours of work, not by hoping for speed.

```
THE CUTS
Revisions 2h -> 1h: reviewer comments live in the doc during drafting,
  so the separate revision pass mostly disappears (−1h)
Design polish 2h -> 1h: house template, no custom layout (−1h)
Revised total: 6 + 5 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 16h = capacity exactly ✓

THE SCHEDULE
Tue eve (2h):  Analysis 2h
Wed (6h):      Analysis 4h (done: 6h ✓) + Drafting 2h
Thu (8h):      Drafting 3h (done: 5h ✓) 09:00–12:00
               Review 3h 12:00–15:00
               Revisions 1h 15:00–16:00
               Polish 1h 16:00–17:00 — submitted at deadline
```

Sequence check: nothing starts before its input exists — drafting begins Wednesday only after 6 hours of analysis are banked, review Thursday starts the moment drafting ends, and the last hour is polish, the one task that can be truncated live if Thursday wobbles. The risk to name to the client: this plan has zero float, so their Thursday feedback window is the submission itself; if they want a pre-read, it costs the polish hour and the report goes out unpolished but complete.

It's Friday 16:00. The release candidate just failed: a payment retry bug. Fix is estimated at 3 hours, the regression suite takes 4 hours, and Monday's deploy window is 06:00–08:00 with the deploy itself taking 45 minutes. The release was promised to customers for Monday 09:00. Slipping to Tuesday costs a $2,000/day penalty with our biggest client. Decide the weekend.

Work the weekend — the penalty math and the deploy window both say so, and Monday's promise can still be kept exactly.

The plan:
- Saturday 10:00–13:00: the fix (3h).
- Saturday 13:00–17:00: regression suite (4h). Total Saturday: 7 hours with a lunch break inside it, worked by the on-call engineer — book comp time for Wednesday afternoon now, while you're asking.
- Monday 06:00: deploy starts inside the window, done by 06:45. That leaves 75 minutes of window as buffer if the deploy snags.
- Monday 09:00: customers get the release as promised. No announcement of a delay is ever sent, because there isn't one.

The alternative — slip to Tuesday — costs $2,000 in penalty plus the credibility of a promise broken by a day for a bug you already understand. The one condition on the weekend plan: if Saturday's regression finds a second, related failure, stop and reassess rather than stacking a second fix — at that point the bug isn't the 3-hour bug you planned around, and Tuesday with the penalty becomes the honest option. Tell the client nothing tonight; tell them Monday at 09:00 that it's live.

Hiring panels Friday: 3 candidates. Each needs a technical interview (45 min), a hiring-manager interview (30 min), and a culture interview (30 min). Our technical interviewer just dropped out. Remaining panel: the hiring manager, the culture lead, and a senior engineer who was going to run a separate system-design session — she can take over the technical interviews if we fold system design into them, extending them to 60 minutes. - Candidate 1: 09:00–11:00 (tech 09:00–10:00, HM 10:00–10:30, culture 10:30–11:00)

Both waves clear — but only if the heavy orders are done while all three pickers are still in the building.

```
